chapters.title: And He Called
chapters.html:
Leviticus 1

From the Herd

1And He called to Moses, and the LORD spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying,

2"Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When any of you brings an offering to the LORD, you shall bring your offering from the livestock — from the herd or from the flock.

3If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall bring an unblemished male. He shall bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting, for his acceptance before the LORD.

4And he shall lean his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it will be accepted for him, to make atonement for him.

5And he shall slaughter the young bull before the LORD, and the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall bring the blood and dash the blood against the altar all around, the altar at the entrance of the tent of meeting.

6And he shall skin the burnt offering and cut it into its pieces.

7And the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire on the altar and lay out wood on the fire.

8And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall lay out the pieces, the head and the suet, on the wood that is on the fire that is on the altar.

9And its entrails and its legs he shall wash with water, and the priest shall turn all of it into smoke on the altar — a burnt offering, an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

From the Flock

10And if his offering is from the flock, from the sheep or from the goats, for a burnt offering, he shall bring an unblemished male.

11And he shall slaughter it on the north flank of the altar before the LORD, and the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall dash its blood against the altar all around.

12And he shall cut it into its pieces, with its head and its suet, and the priest shall lay them out on the wood that is on the fire that is on the altar.

13And the entrails and the legs he shall wash with water, and the priest shall bring all of it and turn it into smoke on the altar. It is a burnt offering, an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

From the Birds

14And if his offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, he shall bring his offering from the turtledoves or from the young pigeons.

15And the priest shall bring it to the altar and pinch off its head and turn it into smoke on the altar, and its blood shall be drained out against the wall of the altar.

16And he shall remove its crop with its feathers and throw it beside the altar, on the east side, at the place of the ashes.

17And he shall tear it open by its wings without severing it, and the priest shall turn it into smoke on the altar, on the wood that is on the fire. It is a burnt offering, an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

Notes

  • v1 "And He called" — va-yiqra, a verb with no subject named, and it is the first word of the book. Hebrew tradition titles books by their opening words, so this book is simply called Vayiqra, And He Called. The English name comes from the Greek by way of the Latin and means about the Levites, which is a description of the contents; the Hebrew name is the first thing that happens in it.

  • v1 and it answers the last verse of Exodus — Exodus closed with Moses could not come into the tent of meeting, because the cloud had settled on it (40:35). The man who built the tent was shut out of it. The next sentence in the Bible is this one: he is called, and the voice comes to him from the tent of meeting. The problem at the end of one book is solved in the first four words of the next, and neither book says so.

  • v2 "when any of you" — adam ki yaqriv mikkem, and adam is the word from the first chapters of Genesis: the human being, the one made from adamah, the ground. Hebrew has ish for a man and could have used it. The sacrificial law opens by addressing the species.

  • v2 "offering" — qorban, from qarav, to come near. The causative hiqriv — used four times in this chapter — means to bring something near. A sacrifice in Hebrew is not named for what happens to it; it is named for what it is for. It is the thing you bring near with, because you cannot go near yourself.

  • v3 "burnt offering" — olah, from alah, to go up. Not named for burning but for rising: the whole animal goes up in smoke and nothing comes back down to the table. It is the only offering in the system where the worshipper eats none of it.

  • v3 "for his acceptance before the LORD" — li-rtsono, and the pronoun is not fixed. It can mean for his acceptance — so that God will receive him — or of his own will, voluntarily. Hebrew grammar allows either and the verse does not choose. Both readings are about the same question: whose willingness is at stake.

  • v4 "he shall lean his hand" — ve-samakh yado, and samakh is not a touch. It is the verb for putting weight on a thing: leaning on a wall, propping something up. The hand does not rest on the head, it presses.

  • v5 who does the killing — the verbs in vv3–6 have one subject, the man who brought the animal: he shall bring, he shall lean his hand, he shall slaughter, he shall skin it, he shall cut it into its pieces. The priests take over only at the blood. An Israelite with a bull at the tent door cuts its throat himself, in front of everyone, and then butchers it. Nothing in the chapter is done on his behalf until the blood is in a bowl.

  • v9 "a soothing aroma" — reiach nichoach, from nuach, to rest, to settle. The first time this phrase occurs in the Bible is Genesis 8:21, when Noah comes out of the ark and burns offerings, and God smells it and resolves never again to curse the ground. The man's name, Noach, is built from the same three letters — though Genesis 5:29 explains it from a different root, nacham, to comfort. The smell is one that settles: it is not a fragrance, it is a subsiding.

  • v11 "the north flank of the altar" — yerekh ha-mizbeach, the thigh of the altar, the same noun that is the hip joint at Genesis 32:25 and the side of the dwelling at Exodus 40:22. Hebrew gives built things bodies as a matter of course.

  • v15 "pinch off its head" — malaq, a verb that occurs twice in the Hebrew Bible, here and at 5:8, and both times of a bird's neck. 5:8 adds the detail that fixes it: at the back of its neck, and he shall not sever it. The head is opened from the bird, not taken off it. This whole section is the poor man's version of the same rite — a bird instead of a bull — and it is given the same closing sentence, word for word, as the bull in v9.

chapters.title: The Offering Without Blood
chapters.html:
Leviticus 2

Flour, Oil, Frankincense

1And when a person brings an offering of a grain offering to the LORD, his offering shall be fine flour, and he shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it.

2And he shall bring it to Aaron's sons, the priests, and one shall scoop out from it his handful of its fine flour and of its oil, with all its frankincense, and the priest shall turn its memorial portion into smoke on the altar — an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

3And what is left of the grain offering shall be Aaron's and his sons' — most holy, from the offerings by fire of the LORD.

Baked, Griddled, Panned

4And when you bring an offering of a grain offering baked in an oven, it shall be unleavened loaves of fine flour mixed with oil, or unleavened wafers spread with oil.

5And if your offering is a grain offering on a griddle, it shall be fine flour mixed with oil, unleavened.

6Break it into pieces and pour oil on it. It is a grain offering.

7And if your offering is a grain offering in a pan, it shall be made of fine flour with oil.

8And you shall bring the grain offering that is made from these to the LORD, and present it to the priest, and he shall bring it near to the altar.

9And the priest shall lift up from the grain offering its memorial portion and turn it into smoke on the altar — an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

10And what is left of the grain offering shall be Aaron's and his sons' — most holy, from the offerings by fire of the LORD.

What May Not Go Up, and What Must

11No grain offering that you bring to the LORD shall be made with leaven, for you shall not turn any sourdough or any honey into smoke as an offering by fire to the LORD.

12As an offering of firstfruits you may bring them to the LORD, but they shall not go up on the altar for a soothing aroma.

13And every offering of your grain offering you shall salt with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant of your God be missing from your grain offering. With all your offerings you shall bring salt.

14And if you bring a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, you shall bring fresh ears roasted in fire, crushed grain of the fresh ear, as your grain offering of firstfruits.

15And you shall put oil on it and lay frankincense on it. It is a grain offering.

16And the priest shall turn its memorial portion into smoke — from its crushed grain and from its oil, with all its frankincense — an offering by fire to the LORD.

Notes

  • v1 "grain offering" — minchah, and the word has nothing to do with grain. It means a gift, and specifically the kind of gift that acknowledges a difference in rank: what a subject sends a king, what Jacob sends ahead to Esau. The first two occurrences in the Bible are Genesis 4:3–5, where Cain brings a minchah of the fruit of the ground and Abel brings one from his flock — the same noun covers both, and it is the word the whole quarrel turns on. By the time it reaches this chapter it has narrowed to the bloodless offering, but it still means tribute.

  • v1 "a person" — nefesh, where 1:2 had adam. Nefesh is the breath, the life, the throat — the word rendered soul in most English Bibles and never meaning a spirit separable from a body. The animal chapter addresses the human being; the flour chapter addresses the appetite.

  • v2 "its memorial portion" — azkarah, from zakhar, to remember, and the noun occurs only in the sacrificial laws. It is the handful that goes into the fire while the rest goes to the priests, and the name does not say whose memory it serves. Either God is being reminded of the giver, or the giver is reminding himself. The word is built so that both fit, and nothing in the law decides it.

  • v3 "most holy" — qodesh qadashim, holiness of holinesses, the same construction applied to the altar at Exodus 40:10 and the name of the inner room. It is said here of a priest's dinner. The leftovers of a bag of flour carry the highest grade of holiness the system has.

  • v6 "Break it into pieces" — patot otah pittim, literally crumble it crumbs: the verb takes its own noun, which is how Hebrew presses a word and how English only stutters. The noun pat survives as the ordinary word for a morsel of bread — a pat of bread is what Abraham offers the three men at Genesis 18:5.

  • v11 "no leaven… and no honey" — two things banned from the fire, and neither is explained. Both are agents of fermentation; both make dough rise and go sour on their own. Devash covers bee honey and thick fruit syrup alike. What the verse forbids is not sweetness or sourness but what they do — the altar takes nothing that changes by itself.

  • v12 what is brought but not burned — the same leaven and honey may be presented as an offering of firstfruits; they simply do not go up on the altar. Two verses, and the distinction they draw is one an English reader can miss entirely: a thing can be given to the LORD and still be wrong to burn.

  • v13 "the salt of the covenant of your God" — stated three times in one verse, from three directions: salt your offering, do not let the salt be missing, bring salt with everything. No reason is given and no story is attached. Salt is the preservative that stops exactly what leaven and honey start, which sets the verse directly against v11 — but the text calls it a covenant rather than a preservative, and leaves the phrase standing with no explanation anywhere in the Torah.

  • v14 "fresh ears roasted in fire" — aviv, the barley at the green stage, before it hardens. It is also a month: the month of Aviv, the one Israel left Egypt in (Exodus 34:18), named for the condition of the grain when the year turns. So the firstfruits offering here and the calendar itself are named by the same word, and the month is measured by a crop rather than by a number.

chapters.title: The Peace Offering
chapters.html:
Leviticus 3

From the Herd

1And if his offering is a peace offering — if he is bringing it from the herd, whether male or female, he shall bring it unblemished before the LORD.

2And he shall lean his hand on the head of his offering and slaughter it at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall dash the blood against the altar all around.

3And he shall bring from the peace offering an offering by fire to the LORD: the fat that covers the entrails, and all the fat that is on the entrails,

4and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, which is on the loins; and the lobe on the liver, which he shall remove with the kidneys.

5And the sons of Aaron shall turn it into smoke on the altar, on top of the burnt offering that is on the wood that is on the fire — an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

From the Flock

6And if his offering for a peace offering to the LORD is from the flock, male or female, he shall bring it unblemished.

7If he is bringing a sheep as his offering, he shall bring it before the LORD,

8and he shall lean his hand on the head of his offering and slaughter it before the tent of meeting, and the sons of Aaron shall dash its blood against the altar all around.

9And he shall bring from the peace offering an offering by fire to the LORD: its fat — the whole fat tail, which he shall remove close to the backbone — and the fat that covers the entrails, and all the fat that is on the entrails,

10and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, which is on the loins; and the lobe on the liver, which he shall remove with the kidneys.

11And the priest shall turn it into smoke on the altar — food, an offering by fire to the LORD.

A Goat

12And if his offering is a goat, he shall bring it before the LORD,

13and he shall lean his hand on its head and slaughter it before the tent of meeting, and the sons of Aaron shall dash its blood against the altar all around.

14And he shall bring from it his offering, an offering by fire to the LORD: the fat that covers the entrails, and all the fat that is on the entrails,

15and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, which is on the loins; and the lobe on the liver, which he shall remove with the kidneys.

16And the priest shall turn them into smoke on the altar — food, an offering by fire, for a soothing aroma. All fat belongs to the LORD.

17A lasting statute through your generations, in all your settlements: you shall eat no fat and no blood.

Notes

  • v1 "peace offering" — zevach shelamim, and the second word is built on the root behind shalom. That root is not primarily about the absence of conflict; it is about a thing being whole, complete, paid up, settled. So the name has been rendered peace offering, offering of well-being, and fellowship offering, and each catches part of it. What separates this sacrifice from the two before it is what happens to the meat: the burnt offering goes up entirely, the grain offering feeds the priests, and this one is the offering the worshipper and his household sit down and eat (7:15–16). The fat and the blood go to the altar; the rest is dinner.

  • v1 "whether male or female" — the burnt offering must be a male, stated twice in chapter 1 (vv3, 10). Here the sex is explicitly optional, and it is the only offering in the opening chapters where the text says so. Nothing is made of it.

  • vv3, 9, 14 "the fat" — chelev, and it is not the fat marbled through meat. It is the hard suet that sheathes the organs — around the entrails, over the kidneys, across the loins — the fat a butcher can lift off in a sheet. That is the portion the altar takes, every time, in all three versions of the rite, and the list is repeated word for word three times so no one can be uncertain which fat is meant.

  • v9 "the whole fat tail" — alyah, the heavy fat-storing tail of the broad-tailed sheep of the region, which can weigh several pounds on its own and was the prized cut. It is named only for the sheep, because only the sheep has one. And he-atseh, the point it is cut at, occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, in this verse, so what exactly it names cannot be recovered — the backbone, the rump, the base of the spine have all been proposed from the anatomy rather than from the word.

  • vv11, 16 "food" — lechem, the ordinary word for bread, and by extension for food in general. The sentence says, flatly, that what goes up off the altar is God's food. The Hebrew Bible uses this language freely in the ritual laws and then turns on it elsewhere in the sharpest terms available: If I were hungry I would not tell you, for the world is Mine and all that fills it. Do I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? (Psalm 50:12–13). Both sentences are in the same book of scripture, and neither is softened to accommodate the other.

  • v16 "All fat belongs to the LORD" — four words in Hebrew, kol chelev la-YHWH, dropped at the end of the ritual instructions with no argument attached. It is the reason for everything the chapter has just described, and it is stated after the fact rather than before.

  • v17 the one line addressed to everybody — the chapter is procedure for priests until this verse, which turns and speaks to the whole population, everywhere they live, permanently: no fat and no blood. Blood is given a reason later (17:11, the life of the flesh is in the blood); the fat never is. Two prohibitions of equal weight in one sentence, and the text explains one of them and not the other.

chapters.title: What Is Done by Mistake
chapters.html:
Leviticus 4

If the Anointed Priest Sins

1And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

2"Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: When a person sins by mistake against any of the commands of the LORD about things that are not to be done, and does any one of them —

3if it is the anointed priest who sins, bringing guilt on the people, then he shall bring for the sin he has sinned an unblemished young bull to the LORD as a sin offering.

4And he shall bring the bull to the entrance of the tent of meeting before the LORD, and lean his hand on the head of the bull, and slaughter the bull before the LORD.

5And the anointed priest shall take some of the bull's blood and bring it into the tent of meeting.

6And the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle some of the blood seven times before the LORD, in front of the veil of the holy place.

7And the priest shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense before the LORD, which is in the tent of meeting; and all the rest of the bull's blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering, which is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.

8And all the fat of the bull of the sin offering he shall lift off it: the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails,

9and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, which is on the loins; and the lobe on the liver, which he shall remove with the kidneys —

10just as it is lifted off the ox of the peace offering. And the priest shall turn them into smoke on the altar of burnt offering.

11But the hide of the bull and all its flesh, with its head and its legs, and its entrails and its dung —

12all the rest of the bull he shall carry outside the camp, to a clean place, to the ash dump, and burn it on wood with fire. At the ash dump it shall be burned.

If the Whole Assembly Sins

13And if the whole assembly of Israel strays, and the matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation, and they do any one of the things the LORD commanded not to be done, and they are guilty —

14when the sin they sinned becomes known, the congregation shall bring a young bull as a sin offering and bring it before the tent of meeting.

15And the elders of the assembly shall lean their hands on the head of the bull before the LORD, and the bull shall be slaughtered before the LORD.

16And the anointed priest shall bring some of the bull's blood into the tent of meeting,

17and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle seven times before the LORD, in front of the veil.

18And he shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar that is before the LORD, which is in the tent of meeting; and all the rest of the blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering, which is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.

19And all its fat he shall lift off it and turn into smoke on the altar.

20And he shall do to the bull as he did to the bull of the sin offering; so shall he do to it. And the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven.

21And he shall carry the bull outside the camp and burn it as he burned the first bull. It is the sin offering of the congregation.

When a Chief Sins

22When a chief sins and does by mistake any one of the things the LORD his God commanded not to be done, and he is guilty —

23or if his sin that he sinned is made known to him — he shall bring as his offering an unblemished male goat.

24And he shall lean his hand on the head of the goat and slaughter it in the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered before the LORD. It is a sin offering.

25And the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and its blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering.

26And all its fat he shall turn into smoke on the altar, like the fat of the peace offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin, and he shall be forgiven.

If One of the People Sins

27And if one person from the people of the land sins by mistake, doing any one of the things the LORD commanded not to be done, and he is guilty —

28or if his sin that he sinned is made known to him — he shall bring as his offering an unblemished female goat for the sin he sinned.

29And he shall lean his hand on the head of the sin offering and slaughter the sin offering in the place of the burnt offering.

30And the priest shall take some of its blood with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and all the rest of its blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar.

31And all its fat he shall remove, as the fat is removed from the peace offering, and the priest shall turn it into smoke on the altar for a soothing aroma to the LORD. And the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven.

32And if he brings a lamb as his offering for a sin offering, he shall bring an unblemished female.

33And he shall lean his hand on the head of the sin offering and slaughter it as a sin offering in the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered.

34And the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and all the rest of its blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar.

35And all its fat he shall remove, as the fat of the sheep is removed from the peace offering, and the priest shall turn them into smoke on the altar, on the offerings by fire of the LORD. And the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin that he sinned, and he shall be forgiven."

Notes

  • vv3, 5, 16 "the anointed priest" — ha-kohen ha-mashiach, and the second word is messiah. It means simply the smeared one, from mashach, to rub oil onto something. In the whole Torah — all five books — the noun occurs in exactly four places, and every one of them is in Leviticus: here three times, and again at 6:22, always of this priest. It is not used of Moses, not of Abraham, not of any king, because there are no kings yet. When it does attach to a king it is in 1 Samuel, of Saul and David, eleven times over. The word an English reader arrives at loaded with expectation enters the Bible as a job description for whoever is currently wearing the oil.

  • v2 "by mistake" — bi-shgagah, from shagag, to stray or wander off. The chapter is about accidents from the first sentence to the last, and there is no provision anywhere in it for a sin committed on purpose. Someone who knew and did it anyway is not addressed here at all — Numbers 15:30 will call that acting with a high hand and give it a different outcome. What this chapter legislates for is the person who finds out afterward.

  • v2 "sins… sin offering" — chata and chatat, the same word. Hebrew uses one noun for the sin and for the animal brought because of it, and the verses switch between the two senses without a marker: slaughter the sin offering in the place of the burnt offering (v29) is literally slaughter the sin. English has to pick a different word each time and loses the identification the Hebrew makes automatically.

  • the descending scale, and how far the blood travels — four cases in one chapter, ranked: the anointed priest, the whole assembly, a chief, one ordinary person. The animal shrinks — bull, bull, male goat, female goat or lamb — and so does the distance the blood is carried. For the first two the priest takes it inside the tent, sprinkles it seven times at the veil and puts it on the incense altar. For the last two it goes no further than the horns of the altar out in the courtyard. The more central the sinner, the deeper into the sanctuary the contamination is treated.

  • v22 "When a chief sins" — the other three cases open with im, if: if the anointed priest sins, if the whole assembly strays, if one person sins. The chief alone gets asher, when. One word, and it is the difference between a possibility and a scheduled event.

  • vv11–12 "outside the camp, to a clean place, to the ash dump" — what is left of the bull after the fat is burned on the altar is not eaten by anybody. It is carted out past the boundary of the settlement and burned on an open fire at the place where the altar ashes are tipped. The text is careful to say that this dump is a clean place, maqom tahor — the carcass is not being disposed of as refuse, and the ground it burns on is not defiled. It is simply not fit to stay inside.

  • vv20, 26, 31, 35 "and they shall be forgiven" — ve-nislach lahem, and the verb is passive with no one named as doing it. The priest is the subject of the sentence before — the priest shall make atonement for him — and then the grammar hands off and nobody is credited with the forgiveness. It reads the same way all four times, at the end of each case, like a stamp.

speech.text: Leviticus 4
If the Anointed Priest Sins
And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,
"Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: When a person sins by mistake against any of the commands of the LORD about things that are not to be done, and does any one of them —
if it is the anointed priest who sins, bringing guilt on the people, then he shall bring for the sin he has sinned an unblemished young bull to the LORD as a sin offering.
And he shall bring the bull to the entrance of the tent of meeting before the LORD, and lean his hand on the head of the bull, and slaughter the bull before the LORD.
And the anointed priest shall take some of the bull's blood and bring it into the tent of meeting.
And the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle some of the blood seven times before the LORD, in front of the veil of the holy place.

And the priest shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense before the LORD, which is in the tent of meeting; and all the rest of the bull's blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering, which is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
And all the fat of the bull of the sin offering he shall lift off it: the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails,
and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, which is on the loins; and the lobe on the liver, which he shall remove with the kidneys —
just as it is lifted off the ox of the peace offering. And the priest shall turn them into smoke on the altar of burnt offering.
But the hide of the bull and all its flesh, with its head and its legs, and its entrails and its dung —
all the rest of the bull he shall carry outside the camp, to a clean place, to the ash dump, and burn it on wood with fire. At the ash dump it shall be burned.
If the Whole Assembly Sins
And if the whole assembly of Israel strays, and the matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation, and they do any one of the things the LORD commanded not to be done, and they are guilty —
when the sin they sinned becomes known, the congregation shall bring a young bull as a sin offering and bring it before the tent of meeting.
And the elders of the assembly shall lean their hands on the head of the bull before the LORD, and the bull shall be slaughtered before the LORD.
And the anointed priest shall bring some of the bull's blood into the tent of meeting,
and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle seven times before the LORD, in front of the veil.

And he shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar that is before the LORD, which is in the tent of meeting; and all the rest of the blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering, which is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
And all its fat he shall lift off it and turn into smoke on the altar.
And he shall do to the bull as he did to the bull of the sin offering; so shall he do to it. And the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven.
And he shall carry the bull outside the camp and burn it as he burned the first bull. It is the sin offering of the congregation.
When a Chief Sins
When a chief sins and does by mistake any one of the things the LORD his God commanded not to be done, and he is guilty —
or if his sin that he sinned is made known to him — he shall bring as his offering an unblemished male goat.
And he shall lean his hand on the head of the goat and slaughter it in the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered before the LORD. It is a sin offering.

And the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and its blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering.
And all its fat he shall turn into smoke on the altar, like the fat of the peace offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin, and he shall be forgiven.
If One of the People Sins
And if one person from the people of the land sins by mistake, doing any one of the things the LORD commanded not to be done, and he is guilty —
or if his sin that he sinned is made known to him — he shall bring as his offering an unblemished female goat for the sin he sinned.
And he shall lean his hand on the head of the sin offering and slaughter the sin offering in the place of the burnt offering.
And the priest shall take some of its blood with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and all the rest of its blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar.

And all its fat he shall remove, as the fat is removed from the peace offering, and the priest shall turn it into smoke on the altar for a soothing aroma to the LORD. And the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven.
And if he brings a lamb as his offering for a sin offering, he shall bring an unblemished female.
And he shall lean his hand on the head of the sin offering and slaughter it as a sin offering in the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered.

And the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and all the rest of its blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar.

And all its fat he shall remove, as the fat of the sheep is removed from the peace offering, and the priest shall turn them into smoke on the altar, on the offerings by fire of the LORD. And the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin that he sinned, and he shall be forgiven."

chapters.title: What a Poor Man Brings
chapters.html:
Leviticus 5

Four Ways to Become Guilty

1And if a person sins — he hears a public call to testify, and he is a witness, whether he saw it or came to know of it — if he does not tell it, he bears his guilt.

2Or a person who touches any unclean thing, whether the carcass of an unclean wild animal or the carcass of unclean livestock or the carcass of an unclean swarming thing, and it was hidden from him, and he is unclean and guilty;

3or if he touches human uncleanness — any uncleanness of a person by which someone becomes unclean — and it was hidden from him, and then he knows, and he is guilty;

4or a person who swears, blurting it out with his lips, to do harm or to do good — whatever a man may blurt out in an oath — and it was hidden from him, and then he knows, and he is guilty in one of these:

5when he is guilty in one of these, he shall confess what he has sinned in,

6and he shall bring his guilt offering to the LORD for the sin he sinned — a female from the flock, a lamb or a female goat, as a sin offering — and the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin.

If His Hand Cannot Reach It

7And if his hand cannot reach the cost of a lamb, he shall bring as his guilt offering for what he sinned two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the LORD, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering.

8And he shall bring them to the priest, who shall present first the one for the sin offering. He shall pinch off its head at the back of its neck without severing it,

9and shall sprinkle some of the blood of the sin offering on the wall of the altar, and the rest of the blood shall be drained out at the base of the altar. It is a sin offering.

10And the second he shall make a burnt offering according to the rule. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin he sinned, and he shall be forgiven.

11And if his hand cannot reach two turtledoves or two young pigeons, he shall bring as his offering for what he sinned a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering. He shall put no oil on it and shall lay no frankincense on it, because it is a sin offering.

12And he shall bring it to the priest, and the priest shall scoop out from it his handful as its memorial portion and turn it into smoke on the altar, on the offerings by fire of the LORD. It is a sin offering.

13And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin he sinned in any one of these, and he shall be forgiven. And it shall be the priest's, like the grain offering.

Against the Holy Things

14And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

15"When a person breaks faith and sins by mistake against any of the holy things of the LORD, he shall bring his guilt offering to the LORD — an unblemished ram from the flock, at your valuation in silver shekels by the shekel of the holy place — as a guilt offering.

16And what he sinned against the holy thing he shall repay, and he shall add a fifth to it and give it to the priest. And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering, and he shall be forgiven.

17And if a person sins and does any one of the things the LORD commanded not to be done, and he did not know it, he is guilty and bears his guilt.

18And he shall bring an unblemished ram from the flock, at your valuation, as a guilt offering, to the priest. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the mistake he made without knowing, and he shall be forgiven.

19It is a guilt offering. He is certainly guilty before the LORD."

Notes

  • v1 the first case is saying nothing — qol alah, the sound of an oath: a public adjuration, someone standing up and calling on anyone who knows something to come forward under oath. A man hears it, has the information, and keeps his mouth shut. That is the opening case of the chapter, and it is a sin of omission — no act is committed, nothing is touched, nothing is said. The list that follows moves from silence to accidental contact to words blurted out, which means the chapter is ordered from the least visible offence outward.

  • v5 "he shall confess" — hitvaddah, from yadah, and this is the first place in the sacrificial system where the offerer has to say anything. Chapters 1 through 4 are entirely hands and knives; the worshipper leans, slaughters, skins, and never speaks. Here, before the animal is brought, he has to state out loud what he did.

  • vv7, 11 "if his hand cannot reach it" — lo taggia yado, literally his hand does not reach, which is what Hebrew says instead of he cannot afford it. The idiom is about grasp, not money, and the chapter uses it twice to build a sliding scale: a lamb, or failing that two birds, or failing that a tenth of an ephah of flour — about two quarts. The rite is written so that nobody is priced out of it.

  • v11 no oil and no frankincense — the grain offering of chapter 2 always carries both, and the reason for stripping them here is given in four words: because it is a sin offering. Oil and incense are the marks of a gift; this is not a gift. So the poorest man's offering is plain flour with nothing added, and the text makes a point of saying it is not being cheapened — the priest handles it exactly as he handles the full version, and it counts exactly the same.

  • v15 "breaks faith" — tim'ol ma'al, the verb with its own noun, which is how Hebrew presses a word. Ma'al is treachery against a trust — it is the word used of a wife suspected by her husband and of Achan taking what was devoted. Applied to the holy things it means using for ordinary purposes something that had been set apart, and the remedy is not only the ram but repayment of the value plus a fifth (v16). This is the one case in the chapter where somebody is out of pocket.

  • v17 guilty without ever knowing — the most uncomfortable sentence in the section: he did not know it, he is guilty and bears his guilt. Guilt here is not a feeling and not a verdict anyone has reached; it is a condition, like a debt accruing on an account nobody has looked at. And v18 has the priest make atonement for a mistake the man still cannot name — for the mistake he made without knowing.

  • v19 "He is certainly guilty" — ashom asham, the verb doubled with its own infinitive, the Hebrew intensifier. And the whole verse is three words long, tacked on after the case has already closed with he shall be forgiven. The chapter ends by restating the guilt of a man it has just declared forgiven, and does not explain why.

  • the two words for the offering — chatat and asham run side by side through this chapter and the verses do not keep them apart tidily: v6 says bring his asham and then calls the animal a chatat. Both nouns mean the wrong and the remedy at once — sin and sin offering, guilt and guilt offering — and where later tradition separates them into two distinct rites, the text here lets them overlap.

chapters.title: The Fire That Does Not Go Out
chapters.html:
Leviticus 6

When the Wrong Is Against a Neighbor

1And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

2"When a person sins and breaks faith with the LORD — he lies to his neighbor about something left in his keeping, or a pledge, or something he seized by force; or he has defrauded his neighbor;

3or he found something lost and lied about it, and swore falsely — in any one of all the things a man may do and sin by doing:

4when he sins and is guilty, he shall give back what he seized by force, or what he took by fraud, or what was left in his keeping, or the lost thing he found,

5or anything at all he swore falsely about. He shall repay it in full and add a fifth to it. He shall give it to its owner on the day of his guilt offering.

6And he shall bring his guilt offering to the LORD — an unblemished ram from the flock, at your valuation — to the priest, as a guilt offering.

7And the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD, and he shall be forgiven for any one of all the things a man may do and incur guilt by."

The Fire That Does Not Go Out

8And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

9"Command Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the instruction for the burnt offering. The burnt offering itself shall stay on the hearth on the altar all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall be kept burning on it.

10And the priest shall put on his linen robe, and put linen undergarments on his body, and lift off the ashes that the fire has made of the burnt offering on the altar, and put them beside the altar.

11And he shall take off his garments and put on other garments, and carry the ashes outside the camp, to a clean place.

12And the fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it; it shall not go out. And the priest shall burn wood on it morning by morning, and arrange the burnt offering on it, and turn into smoke on it the fat of the peace offerings.

13Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually. It shall not go out.

The Grain Offering, and Who Eats It

14And this is the instruction for the grain offering. Aaron's sons shall bring it near before the LORD, in front of the altar.

15And one shall lift from it his handful — of the fine flour of the grain offering and of its oil, and all the frankincense that is on the grain offering — and turn its memorial portion into smoke on the altar, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

16And what is left of it Aaron and his sons shall eat. It shall be eaten unleavened in a holy place; in the court of the tent of meeting they shall eat it.

17It shall not be baked with leaven. I have given it as their share from My offerings by fire. It is most holy, like the sin offering and like the guilt offering.

18Every male among Aaron's sons may eat it — a lasting statute through your generations, from the offerings by fire of the LORD. Whatever touches them becomes holy."

The Priest's Own Offering

19And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

20"This is the offering of Aaron and his sons that they shall bring to the LORD on the day he is anointed: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a regular grain offering, half of it in the morning and half of it in the evening.

21It shall be made on a griddle with oil. You shall bring it soaked, and present it baked in pieces — a grain offering, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

22And whichever of his sons is anointed priest in his place shall make it. It is a lasting statute: to the LORD it shall go up in smoke whole.

23And every grain offering of a priest shall be burned whole. It shall not be eaten."

The Sin Offering, and What It Touches

24And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

25"Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the instruction for the sin offering. In the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered the sin offering shall be slaughtered, before the LORD. It is most holy.

26The priest who offers it for sin shall eat it. It shall be eaten in a holy place, in the court of the tent of meeting.

27Whatever touches its flesh becomes holy; and if any of its blood is spattered on a garment, you shall wash what it was spattered on in a holy place.

28And an earthen vessel in which it was boiled shall be broken; and if it was boiled in a bronze vessel, that shall be scoured and rinsed with water.

29Every male among the priests may eat it. It is most holy.

30But no sin offering shall be eaten if its blood is brought into the tent of meeting to make atonement in the holy place. It shall be burned in the fire."

Notes

  • the chapter numbers here do not match a Hebrew Bible — the Hebrew divides this material seven verses later than the English does. Hebrew Leviticus 5 runs to twenty-six verses and carries what English prints as 6:1–7; Hebrew chapter 6 then covers English 6:8–30. This rendering follows the English division throughout, so it can be set beside a printed Bible. Anyone checking it against the Hebrew should subtract seven from the verse numbers in the first section and add seven in the rest.

  • v2 "breaks faith with the LORD" — ma'alah ma'al ba-YHWH, the same charge 5:15 brought against a man who misused the holy things. Here nothing holy has been touched. A man has lied to a neighbor about a deposit, or kept something he found, and the text calls it treachery against God — then spends five verses on the neighbor's property and one on the ram. The wrong runs in two directions at once, and the law will not let the vertical one be settled first.

  • v2 "his neighbor" — amito, a word that occurs ten times in the Hebrew Bible: nine of them in Leviticus, and one in Zechariah. It is not the ordinary rea of love your neighbor as yourself (19:18). It means an associate, someone you stand alongside — and the verb used against him here, kachash, to deny or lie about, is the same verb in the same construction at 19:11: you shall not steal, and you shall not deal falsely, and you shall not lie to one another.

  • v2 "a pledge" — tesumet yad, literally a putting of the hand, and the phrase occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. Something handed over and closed on — a security, a deposit held against a debt, goods put into a partner's hands. The three nouns before and after it are ordinary and sharp: pikkadon, what is left in someone's keeping; gazel, what is taken by force. This one sits between them and cannot be pinned down further.

  • v5 "repay it in full" — be-rosho, literally in its head, which is Hebrew for the capital sum as against the interest or the fine. The fifth is added on top of it. And the restitution runs to its owner, not to the sanctuary: of every offering in these six chapters, this is the only one where somebody outside the priesthood is handed anything back.

  • v5 "on the day of his guilt offering" — be-yom ashmato, on the day of his guilt, and the noun means the guilt and the offering brought for it at once. So the sentence either dates the repayment to the day his guilt is established or to the day he brings the ram, and nothing in the verse settles which. Either way the two land together: he cannot pay the man back and leave the altar for later, or square it with God and pay the man when it suits him.

  • vv9, 14, 25 "This is the instruction for" — zot torat, and torah is not primarily a law. It is from yarah, to throw or shoot, and so to point — instruction, direction, what a teacher hands a student. The word that comes into English as the Torah, the name of the whole five books, is used here for the handling procedure of a burnt offering.

  • vv10–11 the ashes — deshen, and it is not the ordinary word for ashes. Deshen is what the fire leaves of fat: the same noun means richness, fatness, the best of a thing everywhere outside the sacrificial laws — they drink their fill of the richness of your house (Psalm 36:8), my soul is satisfied as with fat and rich food (Psalm 63:5), I will saturate the appetite of the priests with richness (Jeremiah 31:14). The first task of the priest's day is carrying out the previous day's residue, and the word for it is the word for abundance.

  • v10 "put on his linen robe" — the priest is dressed in the holy linen to lift the ashes off the altar, and in v11 he changes into other clothes to carry them out of the camp. The garments are graded by where they go, not by the dignity of the job: the same linen undergarments made at Exodus 28:42 are worn for this. Somebody has to empty the fireplace, and the text says who, and what he wears, and where he puts it.

  • vv12–13 "it shall not go out" — said twice in two verses, with tukad, shall be kept burning, three times across vv9–13. The only thing in the entire sanctuary that is commanded to be continuous is the fire, and keeping it so is manual: somebody carries wood every morning. Tamid, continually, is the word that will attach to the lamp, the bread and the daily offering — the standing things — and it gets here first.

  • vv18, 27 "whatever touches them becomes holy" — stated twice, of the grain offering and of the sin offering's flesh, and it runs the opposite way to everything modern intuition expects. Uncleanness is the thing that normally spreads by contact. Here holiness does, and it is not presented as a blessing: v27 continues straight into what to do about blood on your clothes and v28 into smashing the pot it was boiled in. The rule is not that holy things are fragile. It is that they are contagious, and what they touch cannot go back to ordinary use.

  • v21 "soaked, and… baked in pieces" — two words here are barely recoverable. Murbekhet occurs three times in the whole Bible, always of this same flour-and-oil preparation, and means something like stirred or soaked through. Tufinei occurs once — this verse, and nowhere else in Hebrew. The proposals run from a form of afah, to bake, to a word for the broken pieces named in the next breath, and the verse offers nothing to decide between them. What can be said is what the priest is handed: flour, oil, a griddle, and an instruction that has not been fully legible for a very long time.

  • vv22–23 what the priest never eats — the grain offering of an ordinary Israelite is mostly the priests' dinner (vv16–18). The priest's own grain offering goes up whole, kalil, twice in two verses, and the last line of the section shuts the door: it shall not be eaten. The men who live off the altar get nothing back from their own gift, and the only one of them named is Aaron, who has to bring it every day of his life, half in the morning and half at dusk.

  • v26 "the priest who offers it for sin" — ha-mechatte, and the verb is chata, to sin. In this form it reverses: it means to de-sin something, to purge the sin out of it. The same three letters that name the offence name the cure, the wrong and the remedy, and the animal — and the only thing that tells a reader which is meant is the shape of the verb.

"Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the instruction for the sin offering. In the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered the sin offering shall be slaughtered, before the LORD. It is most holy.

Whatever touches its flesh becomes holy; and if any of its blood is spattered on a garment, you shall wash what it was spattered on in a holy place.

chapters.html:
Leviticus 7

The Guilt Offering, and the Priest's Share

1And this is the instruction for the guilt offering. It is most holy.

2In the place where they slaughter the burnt offering they shall slaughter the guilt offering, and its blood shall be dashed against the altar all around.

3And all its fat he shall bring from it: the fat tail, and the fat that covers the entrails,

4and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, which is on the loins; and the lobe on the liver, which he shall remove with the kidneys.

5And the priest shall turn them into smoke on the altar, an offering by fire to the LORD. It is a guilt offering.

6Every male among the priests may eat it. It shall be eaten in a holy place. It is most holy.

7The sin offering and the guilt offering have one instruction between them: it belongs to the priest who makes atonement with it.

8And the priest who presents any man's burnt offering — the hide of the burnt offering he presented belongs to that priest himself.

9And every grain offering baked in an oven, and everything made in a pan or on a griddle, belongs to the priest who presents it.

10And every grain offering mixed with oil, or dry, belongs to all the sons of Aaron alike.

The Thanksgiving Offering

11And this is the instruction for the peace offering that a man brings to the LORD.

12If he brings it for thanksgiving, he shall bring with the thanksgiving sacrifice unleavened loaves mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers spread with oil, and loaves of fine flour soaked and mixed with oil.

13He shall bring his offering with loaves of leavened bread, along with his thanksgiving peace offering.

14And from it he shall bring one of each kind as a contribution to the LORD. It belongs to the priest who dashes the blood of the peace offering.

15And the flesh of his thanksgiving peace offering shall be eaten on the day it is offered. He shall leave none of it until morning.

16But if the sacrifice he brings is a vow or a freewill offering, it shall be eaten on the day he brings his sacrifice, and what is left of it may be eaten the next day.

17And what is left of the flesh of the sacrifice on the third day shall be burned in the fire.

18And if any of the flesh of his peace offering is eaten at all on the third day, it will not be accepted. It will not be credited to the one who brought it. It is foul, and the person who eats it bears his guilt.

19And flesh that touches anything unclean shall not be eaten; it shall be burned in the fire. As for the flesh, anyone who is clean may eat it.

20But the person who eats flesh from the peace offering that belongs to the LORD while his uncleanness is on him — that person shall be cut off from his people.

21And when a person touches anything unclean — human uncleanness, or an unclean animal, or any unclean swarming thing — and eats flesh from the peace offering that belongs to the LORD, that person shall be cut off from his people."

No Fat and No Blood

22And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

23"Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: You shall eat no fat of ox or sheep or goat.

24The fat of an animal that died on its own, and the fat of one torn by beasts, may be put to any use, but you shall certainly not eat it.

25For anyone who eats the fat of an animal from which an offering by fire is brought to the LORD — the person who eats it shall be cut off from his people.

26And you shall eat no blood at all, in any of your settlements, whether of bird or of animal.

27Any person who eats any blood — that person shall be cut off from his people."

The Breast and the Right Thigh

28And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

29"Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: Whoever brings his peace offering to the LORD shall bring his offering to the LORD from his peace offering.

30His own hands shall bring the offerings by fire of the LORD. He shall bring the fat with the breast, the breast to be waved before the LORD.

31And the priest shall turn the fat into smoke on the altar, and the breast shall be Aaron's and his sons'.

32And the right thigh you shall give to the priest as a contribution from your peace offerings.

33The one among Aaron's sons who presents the blood of the peace offering and the fat — the right thigh shall be his as his share.

34For the breast that is waved and the thigh that is lifted off I have taken from the sons of Israel, from their peace offerings, and I have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons as a lasting due from the sons of Israel.

35This is the share that comes with the anointing of Aaron and the anointing of his sons, out of the offerings by fire of the LORD, from the day they were brought forward to serve the LORD as priests —

36which the LORD commanded to be given them by the sons of Israel on the day He anointed them, a lasting statute through their generations.

37This is the instruction for the burnt offering, the grain offering, the sin offering, the guilt offering, the ordination offering, and the peace offering,

38which the LORD commanded Moses on Mount Sinai on the day He commanded the sons of Israel to bring their offerings to the LORD, in the wilderness of Sinai.

Notes

  • v12 "thanksgiving" — todah, from yadah, and it is the same root as hitvaddah, to confess, at 5:5. One verb covers both: the sacrifice for which a man says what God has done for him, and the act by which he says what he has done himself. Joshua uses it of Achan — give praise to the LORD the God of Israel and make confession to Him (Joshua 7:19) — where a single Hebrew root does the work of both English words in one breath. Owning the good and owning the wrong are not separate motions in this language.

  • v15 eaten in a day — the thanksgiving offering must be finished before morning; the vow and the freewill offering get two days (v16). This is the tightest deadline in the sacrificial laws and it has a practical consequence the text does not spell out: an ox and four kinds of bread cannot be eaten by one household between afternoon and dark. The rule does not say invite people. It makes it impossible not to.

  • v13 the one leavened thing on the list — leaven is banned from the altar outright (2:11), and here the thanksgiving offering arrives with leavened loaves. They are not burned. They come with the meal and go to the priest and the table, and the prohibition holds exactly where it was drawn: at the fire, not at the feast.

  • v10 "alike" — ish ke-achiv, a man like his brother, which is Hebrew for share and share alike. It is the one line in the chapter that divides something equally: the baked and griddled grain offerings go to whichever priest handled them (v9), the hide goes to whoever presented the animal (v8), and the plain flour, cooked by nobody, is split evenly among all of them.

  • v18 "It is foul" — piggul, a word that occurs four times in the Hebrew Bible and never with an explanation: here, at 19:7 of the same third-day meat, in Ezekiel 4:14 of food a priest refuses to put in his mouth, and in Isaiah 65:4 of what is being boiled in the pots of people sitting among graves. Every one of the four is about something eaten. It is the strongest available word for food that has gone wrong, and the law applies it to meat that was holy two days earlier.

  • v18 "eaten at all" — he'akhol ye'akhel, the verb doubled with itself, which is how Hebrew leans on a word. The doubling is not thoroughly eaten or eaten up; it closes off the excuses — a mouthful is eating.

  • v18 "will not be credited" — lo yechashev lo, from chashav, the accounting verb: to reckon, to enter in a ledger. It is the verb of Genesis 15:6, where Abraham's trust was credited to him as righteousness. Here it runs the other way. A man brought a whole animal, did every step correctly, and three days later the entry is struck out over how the leftovers were handled.

  • vv20, 21, 25, 27 "cut off from his people" — ve-nikhretah, from karat, the verb for cutting — and the same verb used for making a covenant, which in Hebrew is cut rather than made. What the penalty actually consists of is never stated anywhere in the Torah: not execution, which the law prescribes plainly where it means it, and not exile, which has its own vocabulary. It is announced four times in eight verses over fat, blood and a meal eaten while unclean, and left undefined.

  • v24 the fat of an animal nobody killed for God — nevelah, one that died on its own, and terefah, one torn by a predator. Their fat may be put to any use — greased, burned for light, worked into something — and only eating it is forbidden. The prohibition of v23 turns out not to be about the substance. Fat is barred because it is the altar's portion; where there was never going to be an altar, the same fat is just material. Terefah is the word behind Jacob's defense to Laban at Genesis 31:39, the standing excuse of a hired shepherd.

  • v30 "his own hands shall bring" — yadav tevi'enah, and the noun is fronted: his hands, they shall bring it. The owner cannot send the fat and the breast up with a servant or hand them over at the gate; the one sentence in this chapter about who physically carries the portion says it is the man himself. Everything else in these chapters is done by priests.

  • v30 "to be waved" — lehanif oto tenufah, to wave it a waving, the verb with its own noun. What the motion was is not described here or anywhere else — extended forward and back, or lifted up and set down, both have been argued from the word. What the text does say is that the waved breast and the lifted thigh are the two cuts that leave the altar and go to the priests' families (v34), and 10:14 will say the daughters eat them too.

  • v32 "a contribution" — terumah, from rum, to be high: the portion lifted off a larger amount and set aside. It is the same verb as lifting the ashes off the altar and lifting the handful out of the flour in 6:10 and 6:15. One motion runs through the whole system — take a part up out of the whole — and the noun built on it becomes the ordinary word for everything given to the sanctuary.

  • v35 "the share that comes with the anointing" — mishchat Aharon, literally the anointing of Aaron, used here for what the anointing pays. The oil is not only a ceremony; it is the instrument of a transfer, and this verse is where the text says out loud that the priesthood is a living. The men have no land (Numbers 18:20). What they have is a standing claim on the breast and the right thigh of every peace offering in Israel.

  • v37 "the ordination offering" — milluim, fillings, from the idiom that names the making of a priest: filling the hand. It is the one item in this closing list with no instructions anywhere behind it — burnt, grain, sin, guilt and peace offerings all have their chapter, and this one does not. Chapter 8 is about to supply it, and there the hands get filled in front of the reader.

chapters.title: The Filling of the Hands
chapters.html:
Leviticus 8

Washed and Dressed

1And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

2"Take Aaron and his sons with him, and the garments, and the anointing oil, and the bull of the sin offering, and the two rams, and the basket of unleavened bread,

3and assemble the whole congregation at the entrance of the tent of meeting."

4And Moses did as the LORD commanded him, and the congregation assembled at the entrance of the tent of meeting.

5And Moses said to the congregation, "This is the thing the LORD has commanded to be done."

6And Moses brought Aaron and his sons forward and washed them with water.

7And he put the tunic on him and tied the sash around him, and clothed him with the robe, and put the ephod on him, and tied the woven band of the ephod around him, fastening it to him.

8And he set the breastpiece on him, and put the Urim and the Thummim into the breastpiece.

9And he set the turban on his head, and on the turban, at the front, he set the gold plate, the holy crown, as the LORD had commanded Moses.

10And Moses took the anointing oil and anointed the dwelling and everything in it, and set them apart.

11And he sprinkled some of it on the altar seven times, and anointed the altar and all its vessels, and the basin and its stand, to set them apart.

12And he poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron's head and anointed him, to set him apart.

13And Moses brought Aaron's sons forward and clothed them with tunics and tied sashes around them and bound caps on them, as the LORD had commanded Moses.

The Bull and the Two Rams

14And he brought the bull of the sin offering, and Aaron and his sons leaned their hands on the head of the bull of the sin offering.

15And it was slaughtered, and Moses took the blood and put it with his finger on the horns of the altar all around, and purified the altar; and he poured out the blood at the base of the altar, and set it apart, to make atonement for it.

16And he took all the fat that was on the entrails, and the lobe on the liver, and the two kidneys and their fat, and Moses turned them into smoke on the altar.

17And the bull and its hide and its flesh and its dung he burned in the fire outside the camp, as the LORD had commanded Moses.

18And he brought the ram of the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons leaned their hands on the head of the ram.

19And it was slaughtered, and Moses dashed the blood against the altar all around.

20And the ram he cut into its pieces, and Moses turned the head and the pieces and the suet into smoke.

21And he washed the entrails and the legs with water, and Moses turned the whole ram into smoke on the altar. It was a burnt offering for a soothing aroma; it was an offering by fire to the LORD, as the LORD had commanded Moses.

Blood on the Ear, the Thumb, the Toe

22And he brought the second ram, the ram of ordination, and Aaron and his sons leaned their hands on the head of the ram.

23And it was slaughtered, and Moses took some of its blood and put it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.

24And he brought Aaron's sons forward, and Moses put some of the blood on the lobe of their right ear, and on the thumb of their right hand, and on the big toe of their right foot. And Moses dashed the blood against the altar all around.

25And he took the fat — the fat tail and all the fat that was on the entrails, and the lobe on the liver, and the two kidneys and their fat — and the right thigh.

26And out of the basket of unleavened bread that was before the LORD he took one unleavened loaf and one loaf of oiled bread and one wafer, and put them on the fat and on the right thigh,

27and he put it all on Aaron's palms and on his sons' palms, and waved them before the LORD.

28And Moses took them from their palms and turned them into smoke on the altar, on top of the burnt offering. They were an ordination offering for a soothing aroma; it was an offering by fire to the LORD.

29And Moses took the breast and waved it before the LORD. From the ram of ordination it was Moses' share, as the LORD had commanded Moses.

30And Moses took some of the anointing oil and some of the blood that was on the altar and sprinkled it on Aaron, on his garments, and on his sons and on his sons' garments with him; and he set apart Aaron, his garments, and his sons and his sons' garments with him.

Seven Days at the Door

31And Moses said to Aaron and to his sons, "Boil the flesh at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and eat it there with the bread that is in the basket of ordination, as I commanded: Aaron and his sons shall eat it.

32And what is left of the flesh and of the bread you shall burn in the fire.

33And you shall not go out from the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days, until the day your days of ordination are complete; for it will take seven days to fill your hand.

34As has been done this day, the LORD has commanded to be done, to make atonement for you.

35And you shall stay at the entrance of the tent of meeting day and night for seven days, and keep the LORD's watch, so that you do not die; for so I was commanded."

36And Aaron and his sons did all the things the LORD had commanded through Moses.

Notes

  • v8 the Urim and the Thummim — they are put into the breastpiece here with no more explanation than Exodus 28:30 gave, and the Bible never provides one. The names are usually connected to or, light, and tam, complete or whole, and they are handled as objects: put in, and later carried, never described. What they did can be partly reconstructed from how they are used elsewhere — a question is asked and an answer comes back one way or the other, and at 1 Samuel 14:37 no answer comes back at all. This verse is the installation of a device whose operation the text assumes everyone knows.

  • v7 "fastening it to him" — the Hebrew verb here is va-ye'efod, made out of the noun ephod: to ephod it onto him. It occurs twice in the Bible, at Exodus 29:5 where the ceremony is prescribed and here where it is carried out, and nowhere else. A garment important enough to have a verb coined for putting it on, and the verb is used only for these two sentences about the same garment on the same man.

  • v10 oil before blood — the first thing Moses does after dressing Aaron is anoint the building: the dwelling, everything in it, the altar seven times over, the basin and its stand. Only then, in v12, does he pour oil on Aaron's head. The structure is made holy before the man who will work in it is, and the man is anointed in the middle of the same operation as the furniture.

  • v15 "purified the altar" — va-yechatte, the verb chata, to sin, in the form that reverses it: to take sin out of a thing. The brand-new altar, which nobody has yet used or defiled, is de-sinned before it is put to work. Holiness in these chapters is not a quality an object has; it is a state something is brought into, and even an unused altar has to be brought there.

  • vv23–24 the ear, the thumb, the toe — tenukh, the soft lobe of the ear, a word that occurs seven times in the Hebrew Bible and nowhere outside two rites: this one, and the restoring of a person healed of a skin disease (14:14, 17, 25, 28). Those two ceremonies are otherwise nothing alike — one installs a man at the center of the camp, the other readmits a man who was living outside it — and they share a gesture found in no other rite: blood on the right ear, the right thumb, the right big toe. Whatever the daub means, the text applies it to going in.

  • v27 "on Aaron's palms" — this is the idiom acted out. Ordination in Hebrew is filling the hand, and here Moses piles fat, the right thigh, a loaf, an oiled loaf and a wafer onto the palms of men who are standing there holding them. Then he takes it all back off and burns it. Their hands are filled with exactly what they will handle for the rest of their lives, and they do not keep any of it.

  • v29 the one portion Moses takes — the breast of the ordination ram goes to Moses. He has performed every action in this chapter: the washing, the dressing, the anointing, the slaughtering, the blood, the burning. He is not a priest and never becomes one; his sons do not inherit anything here. For one day the whole priesthood is a man from the tribe of Levi who will hand it to his brother in the morning and go back to being a prophet.

  • v30 oil and blood together — sprinkled on the men and on their clothes. Every other mixture in these chapters is oil with flour, and blood stays on the altar. Here the two are put on fabric, and the garments are named twice in one verse as things being set apart. What a priest wears is holy in its own right, not by association with him.

  • v31 "Boil the flesh" — and 6:28 has just ruled that the pot a sin offering is boiled in must be smashed if it is clay, or scoured if it is bronze. The law was given two chapters ago and this is the first meal cooked under it. The text moves from the rule to the cooking pot without remarking on it.

  • v33 "for seven days" — they are confined to the doorway, day and night, for a week. Nothing is said about what they do during it. The reason given is not training and not purification: so that you do not die (v35). It is the first time that warning appears in Leviticus, and chapter 10 is two chapters away.

  • v35 "keep the LORD's watch" — u-shmartem et mishmeret YHWH, the verb with its own noun, which is how Hebrew presses a word: keep the keeping. Mishmeret is a guard duty, a watch posted, and the same pairing will describe the Levites' permanent job (Numbers 3:7). The priesthood begins with a week of guard duty at a door, and the thing being guarded is not named.

chapters.title: The Eighth Day
chapters.html:
Leviticus 9

The Eighth Day

1And it came to pass on the eighth day that Moses called Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel.

2And he said to Aaron, "Take for yourself a bull calf for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering, both without blemish, and bring them before the LORD.

3And speak to the sons of Israel, saying: Take a male goat for a sin offering, and a calf and a lamb, both a year old and without blemish, for a burnt offering,

4and an ox and a ram for peace offerings, to sacrifice before the LORD, and a grain offering mixed with oil — because today the LORD is appearing to you."

5And they took what Moses commanded to the front of the tent of meeting, and the whole congregation came near and stood before the LORD.

6And Moses said, "This is the thing the LORD commanded you to do, so that the glory of the LORD may appear to you."

7And Moses said to Aaron, "Come near to the altar and make your sin offering and your burnt offering, and make atonement for yourself and for the people; and make the offering of the people and make atonement for them, as the LORD has commanded."

Aaron's Own Offering

8And Aaron came near to the altar and slaughtered the calf of the sin offering that was his own.

9And Aaron's sons brought the blood to him, and he dipped his finger in the blood and put it on the horns of the altar, and poured out the blood at the base of the altar.

10And the fat and the kidneys and the lobe from the liver of the sin offering he turned into smoke on the altar, as the LORD had commanded Moses.

11And the flesh and the hide he burned in the fire outside the camp.

12And he slaughtered the burnt offering, and Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he dashed it against the altar all around.

13And they handed him the burnt offering piece by piece, with the head, and he turned it into smoke on the altar.

14And he washed the entrails and the legs, and turned them into smoke on top of the burnt offering on the altar.

The People's Offering

15And he brought the people's offering. He took the goat of the sin offering that was for the people, and slaughtered it, and offered it for sin like the first one.

16And he brought the burnt offering and made it according to the rule.

17And he brought the grain offering, and filled his palm from it, and turned it into smoke on the altar, besides the morning burnt offering.

18And he slaughtered the ox and the ram, the people's peace offering, and Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he dashed it against the altar all around,

19and the fat pieces from the ox and from the ram — the fat tail and the covering fat and the kidneys and the lobe of the liver —

20and they put the fat pieces on the breasts, and he turned the fat pieces into smoke on the altar.

21And the breasts and the right thigh Aaron waved before the LORD, as Moses had commanded.

Fire

22And Aaron lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them, and came down from making the sin offering and the burnt offering and the peace offering.

23And Moses and Aaron went into the tent of meeting, and came out and blessed the people; and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people.

24And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the fat pieces on the altar. And all the people saw, and they shouted, and they fell on their faces.

Notes

  • v1 "on the eighth day" — seven days shut in at the doorway (8:33), and this is the morning after. The number is doing what it does everywhere in this book: seven is the full count, and the eighth is when the thing the count was for actually happens. Nothing in chapter 8 was the priesthood working. It was the priesthood being assembled.

  • vv7–8 "the sin offering that was his own" — Aaron's first act as high priest is to kill an animal for his own sin, in front of the whole congregation, before he touches anything belonging to anybody else. The order was set out in v7 and it is not negotiable: make atonement for yourself and for the people, in that sequence. A man who has been a priest for eight days is already assumed to need it.

  • v2 "a bull calf" — egel ben baqar, and egel is calf. The law of chapter 4 requires a bull, par, for the anointed priest's sin offering, and what Aaron is told to bring is a calf. The Torah does not remark on the substitution, and Aaron's last recorded involvement with a calf was Exodus 32, where he made one out of the people's gold and built an altar in front of it. The text puts a calf in his hands on his first day and says nothing.

  • vv12, 13, 18 "handed him" — va-yamtsi'u, from matsa, to find: in this form, to cause something to reach somebody. It is used three times in this chapter and almost nowhere else for passing an object. The picture is of sons working a line — the blood reaching Aaron's hand, then the carcass reaching it piece by piece — with the father never leaving the altar.

  • v17 "filled his palm from it" — va-yemalle khappo, and filling the hand is the idiom for ordaining a priest (8:33). Two verses into his working life, the phrase turns literal and ordinary: he is measuring flour. Whatever was installed in him in chapter 8 now looks like a handful of grain going into a fire.

  • v22 "lifted his hands" — the written consonants of the Hebrew say his hand, singular; the reading tradition preserved alongside them says his hands. Leviticus has only five words where the written and the spoken forms part company, and two of them are this one — here, and at 16:21, where Aaron lays his hands on the head of the goat that carries the people's sins into the wilderness. Both are Aaron's hands, and both are the gesture that moves something between him and the people.

  • v22 the first blessing, with no words — a priest blesses Israel for the first time here and the text does not record what he said. The words are not given until Numbers 6:24–26, two books later — the LORD bless you and keep you — and there they are given as a command to Aaron. Here the blessing simply happens, is not quoted, and is followed by him walking down the ramp.

  • v23 what the blessing does not accomplish — Aaron blesses, and nothing. Then Moses and Aaron go inside together, come out, and bless again, and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people. The text sets the two attempts side by side without explaining the difference, and does not say what the two men did in the tent.

  • v24 "fire came out from before the LORD and consumed" — va-tetse esh mi-lifnei YHWH va-tokhal. The same four words open 10:2, five verses later, where the fire comes out and consumes Nadab and Abihu. Nothing marks the second occurrence as a different kind of event. The same fire that answers the offering here, on the best day of Aaron's life, kills two of his sons on the next page, and Hebrew does not give the reader any warning in the vocabulary.

  • v24 "they shouted" — va-yaronnu, from ranan, a verb for a loud ringing cry, the word behind the shouting in the Psalms. It is not awe and it is not silence. The people yell, and then go face down on the ground.
