chapters.title: Strange Fire
chapters.html:
Leviticus 10

Strange Fire

1And Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu each took his fire pan, and put fire in them, and laid incense on it, and brought near before the LORD strange fire, which He had not commanded them.

2And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, and they died before the LORD.

3And Moses said to Aaron, "This is what the LORD spoke, saying: Through those near Me I will be shown holy, and before all the people I will be honored." And Aaron was silent.

4And Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel, Aaron's uncle, and said to them, "Come near, carry your brothers away from the front of the holy place, outside the camp."

5And they came near and carried them in their tunics outside the camp, as Moses had said.

6And Moses said to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar his sons, "Do not let your hair go loose and do not tear your clothes, or you will die and anger will come on the whole congregation. But your brothers, the whole house of Israel, may weep for the burning the LORD has burned.

7And do not go out from the entrance of the tent of meeting, or you will die, because the LORD's anointing oil is on you." And they did as Moses said.

What the Priests May Not Do

8And the LORD spoke to Aaron, saying,

9"Do not drink wine or strong drink, you or your sons with you, when you come into the tent of meeting, or you will die. It is a lasting statute through your generations,

10and so that you can separate between the holy and the ordinary, and between the unclean and the clean,

11and teach the sons of Israel all the statutes the LORD has spoken to them through Moses."

The Meal That Was Not Eaten

12And Moses spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his remaining sons: "Take the grain offering that is left from the offerings by fire of the LORD and eat it unleavened beside the altar, because it is most holy.

13And you shall eat it in a holy place, because it is your due and your sons' due from the offerings by fire of the LORD; for so I was commanded.

14And the breast that was waved and the thigh that was lifted off you shall eat in a clean place — you and your sons and your daughters with you — because they are given as your due and your sons' due from the peace offerings of the sons of Israel.

15The thigh that was lifted off and the breast that was waved they shall bring with the offerings by fire of the fat pieces, to wave before the LORD; and it shall be yours and your sons' with you as a lasting due, as the LORD has commanded."

16And Moses searched and searched for the goat of the sin offering, and here — it had been burned. And he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's remaining sons, and said,

17"Why did you not eat the sin offering in the holy place? It is most holy, and He gave it to you to carry the guilt of the congregation, to make atonement for them before the LORD.

18Look — its blood was not brought inside the holy place. You should certainly have eaten it in the holy place, as I commanded."

19And Aaron said to Moses, "Look — today they brought their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and things like this have happened to me. If I had eaten a sin offering today, would that have been good in the eyes of the LORD?"

20And Moses heard, and it was good in his eyes.

Notes

  • v1 "strange fire" — esh zarah, and the adjective is already on the books. Exodus 30:9 forbids qetoret zarah, strange incense, on the incense altar, in a verse about equipment written before either man was ordained. What the text never supplies is what made it strange. The only reason given is negative: which He had not commanded them. Not that it was forbidden — that it was not ordered. In a book where every action so far has been prescribed down to which finger, doing something unprescribed turns out to be the offence.

  • vv1, 3, 4 the word that runs through the chapter — qarav, to come near, is the verb behind every offering in chapters 1 through 9: an offering is a qorban, a thing brought near. Here Nadab and Abihu bring near strange fire (v1); Moses says God will be shown holy bi-qrovai, through those near Me (v3); and the cousins who carry the bodies out are told qirvu, come near (v4). The same root covers the offering, the offenders, and the men who clear away what is left.

  • v3 the quotation with no source — Moses says this is what the LORD spoke, and then quotes a sentence that is recorded nowhere in the Torah. The nearest thing to it is Exodus 29:43, and it shall be made holy by My glory — said of the tent, not of people. The verb here, eqqadesh, I will be shown holy, occurs in this form once in the Hebrew Bible, in this verse. Aaron has just lost two sons, and the explanation he is given is a quotation the reader has never been shown.

  • v3 "And Aaron was silent" — va-yiddom Aharon, two words, and it ends the scene. This exact form occurs four times in the Bible, and one of the others is Joshua 10:13, and the sun stood still. The verb is not only about sound; it is about a thing stopping. What Aaron does is not described as grief, acceptance, shock, or protest. He simply comes to a halt, and the text moves on to the disposal of the bodies.

  • v5 "carried them in their tunics" — the garments Moses put on them in 8:13. Whether the tunics are what the bodies were carried in or carried by is not settled by the Hebrew, but either way, the last mention of Nadab and Abihu in the chapter is their priestly clothing, intact. The fire consumed the men and not the uniform.

  • v6 "do not let your hair go loose" — al tifra'u, from para, to unbind or let run wild, and with do not tear your clothes it names the two standard gestures of mourning. Aaron and his two surviving sons are forbidden both, and forbidden to leave the doorway (v7). Their brothers may be wept for by the entire nation — the text says so in the same breath — by everyone except the three men who actually lost them.

  • v6 "anger will come" — yiqtsof, and the Hebrew gives the verb no subject at all: and upon the whole congregation it will be angry. Wrath is spoken of as a thing that arrives rather than as something somebody does. English cannot leave a verb unattached like that, and every translation has to decide whether to supply He. Nothing in the verse supplies it.

  • v9 wine, placed here — the ban on drinking before entering the tent arrives immediately after two priests die doing something unauthorized, and is addressed to Aaron directly — one of very few times in the Torah God speaks to him without Moses. The text does not say Nadab and Abihu had been drinking. It puts the law here, and says nothing.

  • v10 "separate between" — le-havdil, the verb of Genesis 1: God separated light from darkness, the waters from the waters, day from night. It is the work of the first three days, and it is handed here to the priesthood as its job description — holy from ordinary, unclean from clean. What God did to the world, the priest is to keep doing inside the camp.

  • v14 "and your daughters with you" — the breast and the thigh may be eaten by the priest's whole household, daughters included, because they are eaten in a clean place rather than a holy one. The distinction of v10 does immediate work: the most holy portions are restricted to males in the courtyard, and these are not most holy, so the family eats them at home.

  • v16 "searched and searched" — darosh darash, the verb doubled with itself, which is Hebrew leaning on a word. Darash is to seek, inquire, investigate — the verb behind midrash. Moses hunts for the goat, finds it burnt, and loses his temper at the two sons who are left, on the day their brothers died.

  • vv19–20 Aaron answers, and wins — his first words since the silence of v3, and he does not apologize. He points at the day itself: things like this have happened to me — the only phrase in the chapter that comes close to saying what he feels, and it does not name it. Then a question rather than a defense: would that have been good in the eyes of the LORD? And Moses, who has been right about everything since the first chapter, hears it and drops the charge. The book does not say who was correct about the law. It says the argument ended.

chapters.title: Clean and Unclean Creatures
chapters.html:
Leviticus 11

On the Land

1And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them,

2"Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: These are the creatures you may eat out of all the animals on the earth.

3Whatever parts the hoof and has the hoof cleft in two and brings up the cud, among animals — that you may eat.

4But these you shall not eat, of those that bring up the cud or part the hoof: the camel, because it brings up the cud but does not part the hoof — it is unclean for you;

5and the rock badger, because it brings up the cud but does not part the hoof — it is unclean for you;

6and the hare, because it brings up the cud but does not part the hoof — it is unclean for you;

7and the pig, because it parts the hoof and has the hoof cleft in two, but does not chew the cud — it is unclean for you.

8You shall not eat their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses. They are unclean for you.

In the Water

9These you may eat of all that is in the water: anything in the water, in the seas and in the streams, that has fins and scales — those you may eat.

10But anything in the seas and in the streams that does not have fins and scales, among all that swarms in the water and among all the living creatures in the water — they are detestable to you.

11They shall be detestable to you. You shall not eat their flesh, and you shall detest their carcasses.

12Anything in the water that does not have fins and scales is detestable to you.

The Birds

13And these you shall detest among the birds — they shall not be eaten, they are detestable: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture,

14the kite and the falcon of every kind,

15every raven of every kind,

16the ostrich, the nighthawk, the gull, and the hawk of every kind,

17the owl, the cormorant, the great owl,

18the white owl, the pelican, the carrion vulture,

19the stork, the heron of every kind, the hoopoe, and the bat.

Things That Swarm

20Every winged swarming thing that goes on four is detestable to you.

21But these you may eat of every winged swarming thing that goes on four: those that have jointed legs above their feet, for leaping with them on the ground.

22These of them you may eat: the locust of every kind, the bald locust of every kind, the cricket of every kind, and the grasshopper of every kind.

23But every other winged swarming thing that has four feet is detestable to you.

What Touching Them Does

24And by these you will become unclean. Anyone who touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening,

25and anyone who carries any of their carcasses shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening —

26every animal that parts the hoof but does not have it cleft in two, and does not bring up the cud. They are unclean for you; anyone who touches them will be unclean.

27And every creature that goes on its paws, among all the creatures that go on four, is unclean for you. Anyone who touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening,

28and the one who carries their carcasses shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening. They are unclean for you.

29And these are unclean for you among the swarming things that swarm on the ground: the mole, the mouse, the great lizard of every kind,

30the gecko, the monitor lizard, the wall lizard, the skink, and the chameleon.

31These are the unclean for you among all the swarming things. Anyone who touches them when they are dead will be unclean until evening.

32And anything they fall on when they are dead becomes unclean — any vessel of wood, or clothing, or hide, or sackcloth, any vessel that work is done with. It shall be put in water and be unclean until evening, and then it is clean.

33And every earthen vessel that any of them falls into — everything in it becomes unclean, and you shall break it.

34Any food that could be eaten, on which water has come, becomes unclean; and any drink that could be drunk, in any vessel, becomes unclean.

35And anything their carcass falls on becomes unclean. An oven or a stove shall be torn down. They are unclean, and unclean they shall be for you.

36But a spring or a cistern, a gathering of water, stays clean; and whoever touches their carcass in it becomes unclean.

37And if any of their carcass falls on any seed for sowing that is to be sown, it is clean.

38But if water has been put on the seed and part of their carcass falls on it, it is unclean for you.

39And if an animal that you may eat dies, whoever touches its carcass will be unclean until evening.

40And whoever eats from its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening; and whoever carries its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening.

Be Holy

41And every swarming thing that swarms on the ground is detestable. It shall not be eaten.

42Whatever goes on its belly, and whatever goes on four, up to whatever has many feet — every swarming thing that swarms on the ground — you shall not eat them, because they are detestable.

43Do not make yourselves detestable with any swarming thing that swarms, and do not make yourselves unclean by them, and so become unclean.

44Because I am the LORD your God. Set yourselves apart and be holy, because I am holy. And do not make yourselves unclean with any swarming thing that moves on the ground.

45Because I am the LORD who is bringing you up from the land of Egypt, to be God to you. And you shall be holy, because I am holy."

46This is the instruction for animals and birds and every living creature that moves in the water and every creature that swarms on the ground,

47to separate between the unclean and the clean, and between the creature that may be eaten and the creature that may not be eaten.

Notes

  • the chapter never says why — forty-seven verses of lists, and not one reason. Not health, not cruelty, not idolatry, not anything. The only thing resembling an explanation arrives at the very end and is about God rather than about the animals: be holy, because I am holy. Every reason an English reader has probably been given for these rules was supplied by somebody later; the text withholds all of them, and the withholding is deliberate enough to be a feature of the chapter.

  • v3 the two tests — a split hoof and chewing the cud, and an animal needs both. What makes the section memorable is that the four exceptions are argued out loud: camel, rock badger, hare, pig, each with its reason spelled out in the same sentence. The law is not content to list what is banned; it shows its working, and it is the only place in Leviticus that does.

  • v7 the pig — it gets one verse, the same shape as the camel's and the hare's, and not a syllable more. Of all the animals named here it is the one that became the emblem of the whole system, and the text treats it as the fourth item on a list of four. Whatever weight it later carried is not in these words.

  • vv13–19 the birds cannot all be identified — twenty names, and the English in every Bible is a best guess for most of them. Several occur only in this list and its twin at Deuteronomy 14, which gives a translator nothing to work with: a word used twice, in a list, with no description attached. Nesher may be the eagle or the griffon vulture; tachmas, shalakh, racham and dukhifat are essentially unknown. What survives clearly is the shape of the list — birds of prey, carrion birds, water birds — and one creature at the end that is not a bird at all.

  • vv18, 30 the same name in two lists — tinshemet appears in the bird list at v18 and again at v30 among the things that crawl on the ground. It occurs three times in the whole Hebrew Bible, twice in this chapter, in two different categories. English Bibles print two different animals for it, usually an owl and a chameleon, which is a solution rather than a reading. The text uses one word twice and does not remark on it.

  • v19 "and the bat" — the last entry in a list of birds. The text sorts creatures by how they move and where they live, not by anatomy; anything that flies belongs with flying things. The same logic runs through v20, where insects go on four although they have six legs, and v27, where what matters about an animal is that it walks on its paws.

  • vv10, 13, 41 "detestable" — sheqets, and it is not the same word as tamei, unclean. Unclean is a condition, and it can be got rid of: wash, wait until evening, and it is over. Sheqets is a verdict, and the chapter also uses it as a verb — you shall detest them (v11, 13) — which is the only thing in these forty-seven verses commanded as an attitude rather than an act.

  • v20 "goes on four" — insects have six legs. The phrase is not a mistake about anatomy, it is a category: walking on legs rather than standing upright, which is the same distinction v27 draws for animals that go on their paws and v42 draws for whatever goes on its belly. The chapter's categories are ways of moving.

  • v36 "a gathering of water" — miqveh mayim, and the phrase is out of Genesis 1:10: and the gathering of the waters He called seas. Here it names the one thing in the chapter that cannot be made unclean by contact. A pot is smashed, an oven is pulled down, a cistern is fine. The word later becomes the name of the ritual bath, mikveh, built on this verse.

  • v44 "be holy, because I am holy" — the first time this sentence appears in the Bible. Qadosh ani, I am holy, occurs five times in all, and every one of them is in Leviticus. It arrives at the end of a chapter about lizards and fins, and the logic is not that the creatures are evil but that Israel is being made to resemble somebody.

  • v45 "who is bringing you up" — ha-ma'aleh, a participle, not a past tense, and not the usual verb. The standard formula is I brought you out, hotseti, a finished act. Here it is ongoing and it is alah, to go up — the same verb Pharaoh feared at Exodus 1:10 and the one God used to Jacob at Genesis 46:4. The exodus is spoken of as still in progress while the people are standing at Sinai arguing about grasshoppers.

  • v47 "to separate between" — le-havdil, closing the chapter with the verb it was handed in 10:10, which is the verb of the first three days of Genesis. The priest's job and the diet laws turn out to be the same job: keeping apart things that would otherwise run together.

And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them,
"Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: These are the creatures you may eat out of all the animals on the earth.
Whatever parts the hoof and has the hoof cleft in two and brings up the cud, among animals — that you may eat.
But these you shall not eat, of those that bring up the cud or part the hoof: the camel, because it brings up the cud but does not part the hoof — it is unclean for you;
and the rock badger, because it brings up the cud but does not part the hoof — it is unclean for you;
and the hare, because it brings up the cud but does not part the hoof — it is unclean for you;
and the pig, because it parts the hoof and has the hoof cleft in two, but does not chew the cud — it is unclean for you.
You shall not eat their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses. They are unclean for you.
In the Water
These you may eat of all that is in the water: anything in the water, in the seas and in the streams, that has fins and scales — those you may eat.
But anything in the seas and in the streams that does not have fins and scales, among all that swarms in the water and among all the living creatures in the water — they are detestable to you.
They shall be detestable to you. You shall not eat their flesh, and you shall detest their carcasses.
Anything in the water that does not have fins and scales is detestable to you.
The Birds
And these you shall detest among the birds — they shall not be eaten, they are detestable: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture,
the kite and the falcon of every kind,
every raven of every kind,
the ostrich, the nighthawk, the gull, and the hawk of every kind,
the owl, the cormorant, the great owl,
the white owl, the pelican, the carrion vulture,
the stork, the heron of every kind, the hoopoe, and the bat.
Things That Swarm
Every winged swarming thing that goes on four is detestable to you.
But these you may eat of every winged swarming thing that goes on four: those that have jointed legs above their feet, for leaping with them on the ground.
These of them you may eat: the locust of every kind, the bald locust of every kind, the cricket of every kind, and the grasshopper of every kind.
But every other winged swarming thing that has four feet is detestable to you.
What Touching Them Does
And by these you will become unclean. Anyone who touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening,
and anyone who carries any of their carcasses shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening —
every animal that parts the hoof but does not have it cleft in two, and does not bring up the cud. They are unclean for you; anyone who touches them will be unclean.
And every creature that goes on its paws, among all the creatures that go on four, is unclean for you. Anyone who touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening,
and the one who carries their carcasses shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening. They are unclean for you.
And these are unclean for you among the swarming things that swarm on the ground: the mole, the mouse, the great lizard of every kind,
the gecko, the monitor lizard, the wall lizard, the skink, and the chameleon.
These are the unclean for you among all the swarming things. Anyone who touches them when they are dead will be unclean until evening.

And anything they fall on when they are dead becomes unclean — any vessel of wood, or clothing, or hide, or sackcloth, any vessel that work is done with. It shall be put in water and be unclean until evening, and then it is clean.
And every earthen vessel that any of them falls into — everything in it becomes unclean, and you shall break it.
Any food that could be eaten, on which water has come, becomes unclean; and any drink that could be drunk, in any vessel, becomes unclean.
And anything their carcass falls on becomes unclean. An oven or a stove shall be torn down. They are unclean, and unclean they shall be for you.
But a spring or a cistern, a gathering of water, stays clean; and whoever touches their carcass in it becomes unclean.
And if any of their carcass falls on any seed for sowing that is to be sown, it is clean.
But if water has been put on the seed and part of their carcass falls on it, it is unclean for you.
And if an animal that you may eat dies, whoever touches its carcass will be unclean until evening.
And whoever eats from its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening; and whoever carries its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening.
Be Holy
And every swarming thing that swarms on the ground is detestable. It shall not be eaten.
Whatever goes on its belly, and whatever goes on four, up to whatever has many feet — every swarming thing that swarms on the ground — you shall not eat them, because they are detestable.
Do not make yourselves detestable with any swarming thing that swarms, and do not make yourselves unclean by them, and so become unclean.
Because I am the LORD your God. Set yourselves apart and be holy, because I am holy. And do not make yourselves unclean with any swarming thing that moves on the ground.
Because I am the LORD who is bringing you up from the land of Egypt, to be God to you. And you shall be holy, because I am holy."
This is the instruction for animals and birds and every living creature that moves in the water and every creature that swarms on the ground,
to separate between the unclean and the clean, and between the creature that may be eaten and the creature that may not be eaten.

chapters.title: After a Child Is Born
chapters.html:
Leviticus 12

After a Child Is Born

1And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

2"Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: When a woman produces seed and bears a male, she shall be unclean seven days; she shall be unclean as in the days of her monthly separation.

3And on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.

4And for thirty-three days she shall stay in the blood of her purifying. She shall not touch anything holy and shall not come into the sanctuary, until the days of her purifying are complete.

5And if she bears a female, she shall be unclean two weeks, as in her separation; and for sixty-six days she shall stay in the blood of her purifying.

6And when the days of her purifying are complete, for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring a year-old lamb for a burnt offering and a young pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering, to the entrance of the tent of meeting, to the priest.

7And he shall present it before the LORD and make atonement for her, and she shall be clean from the flow of her blood. This is the instruction for the woman who gives birth, to a male or to a female.

8And if her hand cannot find enough for a lamb, she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean."

Notes

  • v2 "produces seed" — tazria, and the verb is the one used of plants. Genesis 1:12: vegetation yielding seed, esev mazria zera, the same stem. Hebrew has ordinary words for conceiving and for becoming pregnant, and the chapter opens with neither. It describes a woman bearing a child in the vocabulary of the third day of creation, and this is the only place in the Torah the verb is used of a person.

  • v3 one verse about the baby — circumcision on the eighth day is dropped into the middle of a law about the mother, in eight Hebrew words, with nothing before or after it. The chapter is not about the child; everything else in it concerns her days, her blood, her offering. The most consequential thing that happens to an Israelite boy gets a subordinate clause, because it is here only to mark where in her count it falls.

  • v4 "the blood of her purifying" — demei tohorah, and it is a strange pair of words. Blood is the substance that makes things unclean everywhere else in Leviticus; here the blood is the purifying. The phrase is not explained, and the situation it describes is neither uncleanness nor cleanness but a third state: she is not contagious any more — nothing here says anyone who touches her is affected — yet she cannot come near what is holy.

  • vv4–5 the count is doubled for a daughter — seven days and thirty-three for a son, fourteen and sixty-six for a daughter. Exactly twice, in both halves. The text gives no reason whatsoever, and none of the reasons later supplied is in the passage. What can be said is what the numbers do: nothing about the child changes, only the length of the mother's separation.

  • v6 a sin offering, for what — she brings a chatat, the offering of chapters 4 and 5, which is brought for a sin committed by mistake. No sin is named here, and nothing in the chapter says she did anything wrong. Whatever the chatat is doing in this law, it is not responding to an act — which is a warning about reading the word sin offering as though it always answered a sin.

  • v8 "if her hand cannot find enough" — lo timtsa yadah, her hand does not find, next to 5:7's lo taggia yado, his hand does not reach. Two different idioms for the same thing in one book, and neither of them mentions money. The sliding scale works the same way it did in chapter 5: the cheaper offering is not a lesser rite, and the verse ends with the identical words the full version ends with — and she shall be clean.

  • v8 and the family in Luke 2 — the Greek of Luke 2:24 quotes this verse: a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. Three verses of that chapter are this law being carried out — circumcision on the eighth day (2:21), the days of purification (2:22), and then the offering, which is the substitute of v8 rather than the lamb of v6. Luke does not comment on which one they brought, and does not need to; anyone who knew this chapter could see it.

chapters.title: The Mark on the Skin
chapters.html:
Leviticus 13

What the Priest Looks For

1And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,

2"When a person has on the skin of his body a swelling or a scab or a bright spot, and it becomes on the skin of his body a mark of blight, he shall be brought to Aaron the priest, or to one of his sons the priests.

3And the priest shall look at the mark on the skin of the body. If the hair in the mark has turned white, and the mark looks deeper than the skin of his body, it is a mark of blight. And the priest shall look at him and declare him unclean.

4But if the bright spot on the skin of his body is white and does not look deeper than the skin, and its hair has not turned white, the priest shall shut the marked man away for seven days.

5And the priest shall look at him on the seventh day, and here — if the mark has stayed as it was and has not spread in the skin, the priest shall shut him away a second seven days.

6And the priest shall look at him again on the seventh day, and here — if the mark has faded and has not spread in the skin, the priest shall declare him clean. It is a scab. And he shall wash his clothes and be clean.

7But if the scab keeps spreading in the skin after he has shown himself to the priest for his cleansing, he shall show himself to the priest a second time.

8And the priest shall look, and here — if the scab has spread in the skin, the priest shall declare him unclean. It is blight.

When It Covers Everything

9When a mark of blight is on a person, he shall be brought to the priest.

10And the priest shall look, and here — if there is a white swelling in the skin and it has turned the hair white, and there is raw flesh in the swelling,

11it is an old blight in the skin of his body, and the priest shall declare him unclean. He shall not shut him away, because he is unclean.

12But if the blight breaks out all over the skin, and the blight covers all the skin of the marked man from his head to his feet, everywhere the priest can see,

13then the priest shall look, and here — if the blight has covered all his flesh, he shall declare the mark clean. It has all turned white; he is clean.

14But on the day raw flesh appears on him he shall be unclean.

15And the priest shall look at the raw flesh and declare him unclean. The raw flesh is unclean; it is blight.

16Or if the raw flesh turns back and becomes white, he shall come to the priest,

17and the priest shall look at him, and here — if the mark has turned white, the priest shall declare the mark clean. He is clean.

A Boil and a Burn

18And when there is a boil on the skin of someone's body and it heals,

19and in the place of the boil there is a white swelling or a reddish-white bright spot, it shall be shown to the priest.

20And the priest shall look, and here — if it looks lower than the skin and its hair has turned white, the priest shall declare him unclean. It is a mark of blight that has broken out in the boil.

21But if the priest looks at it, and here — there is no white hair in it, and it is not lower than the skin, and it is faded, then the priest shall shut him away seven days.

22And if it keeps spreading in the skin, the priest shall declare him unclean. It is a mark.

23But if the bright spot stays where it is and has not spread, it is the scar of the boil, and the priest shall declare him clean.

24Or when there is a burn from fire on the skin of someone's body, and the raw place of the burn becomes a reddish-white or white bright spot,

25the priest shall look at it, and here — if the hair in the bright spot has turned white and it looks deeper than the skin, it is blight that has broken out in the burn. And the priest shall declare him unclean. It is a mark of blight.

26But if the priest looks at it, and here — there is no white hair in the bright spot, and it is not lower than the skin, and it is faded, then the priest shall shut him away seven days.

27And the priest shall look at him on the seventh day. If it keeps spreading in the skin, the priest shall declare him unclean. It is a mark of blight.

28But if the bright spot stays where it is and has not spread in the skin, and it is faded, it is the swelling of the burn, and the priest shall declare him clean, because it is the scar of the burn.

On the Head or in the Beard

29And when a man or a woman has a mark on the head or in the beard,

30the priest shall look at the mark, and here — if it looks deeper than the skin and there is thin yellow hair in it, the priest shall declare him unclean. It is a scaly patch; it is blight of the head or of the beard.

31And when the priest looks at the mark of the scaly patch, and here — it does not look deeper than the skin, and there is no black hair in it, then the priest shall shut the marked person away for seven days.

32And the priest shall look at the mark on the seventh day, and here — if the scaly patch has not spread, and there is no yellow hair in it, and the patch does not look deeper than the skin,

33then he shall shave himself, but he shall not shave the patch; and the priest shall shut the patch away a second seven days.

34And the priest shall look at the scaly patch on the seventh day, and here — if the patch has not spread in the skin and does not look deeper than the skin, the priest shall declare him clean. And he shall wash his clothes and be clean.

35But if the scaly patch does keep spreading in the skin after he has been declared clean,

36the priest shall look at him, and here — if the patch has spread in the skin, the priest does not need to look for the yellow hair. He is unclean.

37But if the patch has stayed as it was and black hair has grown in it, the patch is healed. He is clean, and the priest shall declare him clean.

What Is Not a Mark

38And when a man or a woman has bright spots on the skin of the body, white bright spots,

39the priest shall look, and here — if the bright spots on the skin of their body are a faded white, it is a rash that has broken out in the skin. He is clean.

40And when a man's head loses its hair, he is bald. He is clean.

41And if he loses the hair at the front of his head, he is bald at the forehead. He is clean.

42But if there is a reddish-white mark on the bald head or the bald forehead, it is blight breaking out on his bald head or his bald forehead.

43And the priest shall look at him, and here — if the swelling of the mark is reddish-white on his bald head or his bald forehead, looking like blight on the skin of the body,

44he is a blighted man. He is unclean. The priest shall certainly declare him unclean; his mark is on his head.

Outside the Camp

45And the person who has the blight, who has the mark on him — his clothes shall be torn and his hair shall hang loose, and he shall cover his upper lip and call out, "Unclean! Unclean!"

46All the days the mark is on him he shall be unclean. He is unclean. He shall live alone; his home shall be outside the camp.

On Cloth and on Leather

47And when a garment has a mark of blight on it, whether a wool garment or a linen garment,

48or on the warp or the weft of the linen or the wool, or on leather or on anything made of leather,

49and the mark is greenish or reddish in the garment, or on the leather, or on the warp or the weft, or on any leather object, it is a mark of blight, and it shall be shown to the priest.

50And the priest shall look at the mark and shut the marked thing away for seven days.

51And he shall look at the mark on the seventh day. If the mark has spread in the garment, or in the warp or the weft, or in the leather, whatever the leather is used for, the mark is a malignant blight. It is unclean.

52And he shall burn the garment, or the warp or the weft, in wool or in linen, or any leather object that has the mark on it, because it is a malignant blight. It shall be burned in the fire.

53But if the priest looks, and here — the mark has not spread in the garment, or in the warp or the weft, or in any leather object,

54then the priest shall give orders, and they shall wash the thing that has the mark on it, and he shall shut it away a second seven days.

55And the priest shall look after the mark has been washed, and here — if the mark has not changed its look, and the mark has not spread, it is unclean. You shall burn it in the fire. It is an eaten-through spot, whether on the back of it or on the front.

56But if the priest looks, and here — the mark has faded after it was washed, then he shall tear it out of the garment, or out of the leather, or out of the warp or the weft.

57And if it appears again in the garment, or in the warp or the weft, or in any leather object, it is breaking out. You shall burn in the fire the thing that has the mark on it.

58And the garment, or the warp or the weft, or any leather object that you wash and the mark leaves it, shall be washed a second time, and it is clean.

59This is the instruction for a mark of blight in a garment of wool or linen, or in the warp or the weft, or in any leather object, to declare it clean or to declare it unclean.

Notes

  • v2 "blight" — tsara'at, and it is not leprosy. English Bibles have printed leprosy since the Greek translators reached for lepra, a general word for scaly skin, and Latin and then English took it from them. Read what the chapter actually legislates for: a condition that turns hair white; that can cover a body completely, at which point the person is declared clean (v13); that breaks out in wool, in linen, in leather (vv47–59) and, in the next chapter, in the plaster of a house. No single illness does all of that. At Exodus 4:6 it arrives on Moses' hand and leaves again inside two verses. What the word names is not a diagnosis but a spreading ruin in a surface — skin, cloth, or wall — and the priest's whole job is to decide whether it is spreading.

  • v2 "a mark" — nega, from naga, to touch. The noun is a touch, a stroke — the same verb that ran through chapter 11, where anyone who touches a carcass is unclean until evening. What is on the skin is described as something that has touched the person, not something they have. The chapter uses it forty-seven times.

  • the priest is not a physician — he prescribes nothing. In fifty-nine verses there is no treatment, no ointment, no prayer, no cure. He looks, he waits seven days, he looks again, and he says one of two words: clean or unclean. Nothing here is about making anyone better. It is about deciding what may come near.

  • vv12–13 covered head to foot, and clean — the verse that rules out any reading of this as a contagion law. A man whose skin is entirely white is sent home; a man with one patch of raw flesh is put out (v14). Whatever the priest is looking for, more of it is not worse. The dangerous state is the one in flux — something spreading, something changing — and the moment it stops changing the man is clean, however he looks.

  • v4 "shall shut the marked man away" — hisgir, to close in, and this is the first quarantine in literature that gets a written procedure: seven days, look, seven days again, look. It is not punishment and it is not treatment. It is time, used as an instrument — the law's way of asking a question that only waiting can answer.

  • v30 "a scaly patch" — netek, from a verb meaning to tear or pull away, used of a hair coming out and of a cord snapping. On the head and in the beard the test changes: not white hair but thin yellow hair, and v33 requires the man to shave around the patch and leave the patch itself unshaved, so the priest can see whether its edge has moved. The procedure is designed for a second look a week later.

  • v39 the look-alike that is clean — bohaq, some faded white patchiness of the skin, and the law names it in order to let it go. Two verses later baldness gets the same treatment twice over (vv40–41): he is bald. He is clean. A chapter this severe about what to exclude takes the trouble to say out loud which ordinary things are not it.

  • v45 "Unclean! Unclean!" — the man is made to announce himself. And the two things he must do — torn clothes and loose hair — are the two things Aaron was forbidden at 10:6, in the same words, paro'a and parom. What the high priest may not do in the worst grief of his life is imposed on this man as a permanent condition. He is dressed as a mourner, and the person he is mourning is himself.

  • v46 "He shall live alone" — badad yeshev. Lamentations opens with the same two words turned on a city: How lonely sits the city that was full of people — yashvah vadad ha-ir. The phrase belongs to this law first, and the poet later says of Jerusalem what the law says of one man with a mark on his skin.

  • vv47–59 the same word, on a coat — the section that makes leprosy impossible. A garment gets tsara'at; so do the warp and the weft, and a leather bag; and the procedure is identical to the one for a human being, down to the two seven-day waits. What the cloth gets is called tsara'at mam'eret, a malignant blight, a word used three times in the Bible — twice here and once in chapter 14, of a house.

  • v55 "an eaten-through spot" — pechetet, which occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, in this verse, and is related to a word for a pit or hollow. The sense is that something has gone through the fabric. It is the last technical term the chapter introduces and there is nothing to check it against.

  • what the chapter never says — no cause is given, anywhere. Not sin, not contact, not punishment, not uncleanness caught from someone else. The narratives elsewhere do link it to a person's conduct — Miriam at Numbers 12:10, Uzziah at 2 Chronicles 26:19 — but the law itself is silent, and reading those stories back into it turns a procedure for looking at skin into a verdict on the person, which is the one thing these fifty-nine verses refuse to do.

Outside the Camp
And the person who has the blight, who has the mark on him — his clothes shall be torn and his hair shall hang loose, and he shall cover his upper lip and call out, "Unclean! Unclean!"
All the days the mark is on him he shall be unclean. He is unclean. He shall live alone; his home shall be outside the camp.
On Cloth and on Leather
And when a garment has a mark of blight on it, whether a wool garment or a linen garment,
or on the warp or the weft of the linen or the wool, or on leather or on anything made of leather,
and the mark is greenish or reddish in the garment, or on the leather, or on the warp or the weft, or on any leather object, it is a mark of blight, and it shall be shown to the priest.
And the priest shall look at the mark and shut the marked thing away for seven days.

And he shall look at the mark on the seventh day. If the mark has spread in the garment, or in the warp or the weft, or in the leather, whatever the leather is used for, the mark is a malignant blight. It is unclean.
And he shall burn the garment, or the warp or the weft, in wool or in linen, or any leather object that has the mark on it, because it is a malignant blight. It shall be burned in the fire.
But if the priest looks, and here — the mark has not spread in the garment, or in the warp or the weft, or in any leather object,
then the priest shall give orders, and they shall wash the thing that has the mark on it, and he shall shut it away a second seven days.

And the priest shall look after the mark has been washed, and here — if the mark has not changed its look, and the mark has not spread, it is unclean. You shall burn it in the fire. It is an eaten-through spot, whether on the back of it or on the front.
But if the priest looks, and here — the mark has faded after it was washed, then he shall tear it out of the garment, or out of the leather, or out of the warp or the weft.
And if it appears again in the garment, or in the warp or the weft, or in any leather object, it is breaking out. You shall burn in the fire the thing that has the mark on it.
And the garment, or the warp or the weft, or any leather object that you wash and the mark leaves it, shall be washed a second time, and it is clean.
This is the instruction for a mark of blight in a garment of wool or linen, or in the warp or the weft, or in any leather object, to declare it clean or to declare it unclean.
